teach_overlay.who_card: Sidney Ringer (1835–1910) — British physician and pharmacologist · Willem Einthoven (1860–1927) — Dutch physician and physiologist · Arthur Keith (1866–1955) — British anatomist and anthropologist · Martin William Flack (1882–1931) — British physiologist · Wilson Greatbatch (1919–2011) — American electrical engineer and inventor

Exactes Nat. 6: 625–633 & 1903 Pflügers Arch. 99: 472–480) shows a 2.5-micrometre silver-coated quartz filament stretched between the poles of a 600-pound (270 kg) water-cooled electromagnet deflecting under a 1 mV cardiac current from three salt-water limb buckets (Einthoven's Triangle) to trace the P wave (atrial depolarization), QRS complex (ventricular contraction), and T wave (repolarization).

teach_overlay.detail: Inked Willem Einthoven (1903 Pflügers Arch. 99: 472–480) string galvanometer specification & P-Q-R-S-T wave chart comparing Augustus Waller's sluggish 1887 capillary electrometer (A-B-C-D) against Einthoven's 2.5 µm quartz string galvanometer (P-Q-R-S-T)
teach_overlay.scale: Einthoven's first ECG machine weighed as much as a grand piano, took five people to run, and needed underground telephone wires to carry heartbeats a mile from the hospital — today that same P-Q-R-S-T wave sits on a smartwatch on your wrist
